notes.2a: The most common error was to balance the species without attempting to balance the charges, giving BrO3 - + Br - + 6H + → Br2 + 3H2O, which gained partial credit. Some candidates attempted to balance such equations by adding electrons on the right hand side which was not acceptable.
notes.2b: (i) This was generally well done, although some candidates gave three correct orders without showing their reasoning and thus only partial credit could be awarded. This emphasises the importance of reading the examination paper carefully.
notes.2bii: This was generally well done, although a few rate equations did not have a k, or began k =.
notes.2iii: Many candidates gave correct answers here. A few candidates ignored the instruction to use –1 –9 experiment 1 to calculate k. Some candidates gave units which were missing s or with dm .
notes.3a: (i) This piece of factual knowledge was known by approximately half of all candidates.
notes.3aii: This piece of factual knowledge was known by far fewer candidates. The most common error was to say that degenerate means “split into different energy levels”. 2 2 2
notes.3iii: Many candidates identified the dz as a higher energy orbital, but fewer identified the dx –y .
notes.3b: (i)(ii) This question discriminated well, the formulae of A, B and C and the colours of B and C being pieces of factual knowledge that need to be learned.
notes.3biii: Many candidates referred to oxidation or reduction rather than redox. In an organic reaction an answer such as oxidation or reduction is often acceptable as it can sometimes be assumed to refer to the organic reactant, but this assumption cannot be made in this case where all species are inorganic. Various incorrect answers for the role of copper metal were seen, such as ligand exchange and oxidising agent.
notes.3c: A surprising number of candidates thought that copper was not a transition element, or stated that because there were no ligands co-ordinated to the metal, the d orbitals did not split. One unfortunate but quite common error was to describe Cu as having “a full d orbital”. This term can 2+ + equally be applied to Cu . Candidates should have described Cu as having “a full d subshell”.
notes.3d: A significant few mistook the absorbance at red and blue as the colour that would be seen. Some candidates mentioned the absorbance of only red or blue instead of both. It was not enough to say “green is not absorbed” since this is also true of white objects.
notes.4a: Most candidates appreciated the significance of HCl being a “stronger acid” or “more dissociated”. Fewer candidates related the strength of acid to the higher concentration of ions, instead referring to more electrons flowing through the wires. While this answer is true it was considered to be an insufficient response. Some candidates referred to electrode potentials and others to the chloride ion’s electron withdrawing effect.
notes.4b: (ii) Many correct answers were possible here, and many were seen. Many candidates suggested NaOH but did not recognise that an excess of ethanoic acid was required compared to the amount of NaOH added. Some candidates did not recognise the need for a “named base” and suggested adding “a base” or “hydroxide”.
notes.4c: This question discriminated well. Correct answers all began with either CH3CH(NH2)CO2H or + – – CH3CH(NH3 )CO2 . A significant number of incorrect answers began with CH3CH(NH2)CO2 or CH3CH(NH3 )CO2H, however these species will be in low concentration in a solution of alanine.
notes.4d: (i) Very few correct answers were seen here. Overall, candidates found this the most difficult question on the paper. Many equations were seen in which a tartaric acid molecule ionised to give a 2– ion and two H ions. This showed incorrect understanding of the dissociation constant.
notes.4dii: A pleasing number of candidates gained full credit here. The most common errors were: • to redraw the structure in the question, • to draw structural isomers not stereoisomers, • to draw a structure in which one or both ends of the molecule was rotated but not different, • to draw two identical structures.
notes.5a: Candidates were not confident in their knowledge of the bonding and shape of benzene. It was hoped that candidates would show the circles of π electron density above and below the plane of the ring, which some did. A surprising number of candidates described the Kekulé structure. Some candidates described the reactivity of benzene, rather than the bonding and shape.
notes.5b: Many candidates made a reasonable attempt at this question, being awarded at least half the credit available. • X was often given correctly as Na or NaOH and correct structures were drawn. • Y was less often correct, but HCl or Na2CO3 followed by correct structures was seen on many scripts. • Z was least often correct. Candidates who chose 2,4-DNPH often found the structure of the product difficult to draw correctly. Candidates who chose an oxidising agent such as 2– + Cr2O7 / H or Tollens’ reagent were most likely to gain credit.
notes.6a: (i) While this was straightforward it required a good understanding of skeletal formulae and of the benzene ring.
notes.6aii: Despite there being only one chiral centre present, a few candidates circled more than one atom.
notes.6iii: Some candidates did not read “in addition to the aryl” group and listed benzene as a functional group. The most common errors were to give amide instead of amine and to give carbonyl instead of ketone.
notes.6b: This question required some standard pieces of factual knowledge, but the novel context of methoxetamine made it difficult for many. In (ii), care and precision were required; one H and a plus charge should have been added to the nitrogen atom. Many answers were seen where either the H or the plus charge were added, but not both. In (iii) the correct structure of the product was most clearly shown by candidates who chose to do partly displayed formulae. Some candidates who chose other approaches often gave ambiguous structures such as –CH3CONCH2CH3 or –NCH3COCH2CH3.
notes.7a: Partial credit was most commonly awarded because candidates often omitted a reference to equilibrium.
notes.7b: (c) These questions were demanding but it is pleasing to note the significant number of candidates gaining full credit.
notes.7d: (i) Most candidates correctly wrote “the solvent” or named a suitable solvent such as water or ethanol. Some candidates wrote “the water between the cellulose fibres” which was not acceptable.
notes.7dii: Several descriptions such as “non-volatile oil” were acceptable but they were rarely seen.
notes.7iii: Many candidates knew that 1 was Rf or retardation factor, fewer candidates knew that 2 was retention time. However credit was often awarded for a correct description of timing that did not use the term “retention time”.
notes.8a: This was correctly answered by most candidates.
notes.8b: Candidates seemed to have difficulty making their answers clear in (i). Many candidates gained credit in (ii) for knowing that the other optical isomer might be toxic, or give side effects, or be harmful in some other reasonable way.
notes.8c: (i) This question discriminated well. Many candidates drew four clear diagrams of the different aldehydes. Common errors were • drawing ketones not aldehydes, • drawing aldehydes that had alkene groups and therefore were not C5H10O, • drawing the same aldehyde more than once.
notes.8cii: (iii) A significant number of candidates stated that CH3(CH2)3CHO has two absorptions; they did not appreciate the different environments in the CH3(CH2)3 chain.
notes.9a: This piece of factual knowledge was known by few candidates.
notes.9b: This was answered well by many candidates although errors included • drawing only one repeat unit, • using the single monomer H2NC6H4CO2H, • drawing the side groups 1,4 on each benzene ring, not 1,3, • missing hydrogen atoms in the amide links, • drawing some correct amide links but drawing others with –O– bonds.
notes.9c: Many candidates answered this correctly. However, a significant number stated that “the primary structure is the peptide link”, which did not receive credit.
notes.9d: Most candidates gained credit for “hydrogen bond”, but few actually drew a correct hydrogen bond. Where the question states “use the diagram” this should always be done in the answer.
notes.9e: These pieces of factual knowledge were known by only a minority of candidates. Some candidates gave answers that restated the question e.g. “heating to 70 C would denature an enzyme” without explaining how.
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates are reminded of the importance of careful, thorough reading of the question before
attempting to answer it.
• Candidates should also be reminded of the need to re-visit and revise AS material while preparing for
the A Level examination.
notes.general_comments:
This examination paper produced many excellent candidate scripts, which were characterised by good
factual knowledge and the ability to apply knowledge and understanding to novel situations.
